passage:
Hi Jeevan,
You won't believe what popped up on my phone yesterday: a message saying I had won a laptop in a lucky draw, and to collect it I only had to pay a small handling fee and read out the code that would arrive by SMS. My heart was doing cartwheels. My thumb was already over the reply button.
Then I remembered our class talk: a genuine prize never wants a fee or a secret code. That code was an OTP! I put the phone down and told Baba. He called the bank straight away, and we blocked the number. He wasn't cross at all.
Say hi to your dad from me.
Anirban

qa.q: What did the message ask Anirban to pay and read out?
qa.a: It asked for a small handling fee and the code that would arrive by SMS.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when the message arrived, and what made Anirban stop?
qa.a: Anirban's heart was doing cartwheels with excitement, but remembering from class that a genuine prize never wants a fee or a secret code made Anirban stop.

qa.q: What should Anirban do if such a message arrives again?
qa.a: Anirban should not share any OTP or pay a fee, and should tell a parent straight away.

qa.q: How might Baba have felt when Anirban told him?
qa.a: Baba wasn't cross, which suggests he was relieved and glad that Anirban told him quickly instead of hiding it.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising a prize scam asking for a fee and an OTP, and telling a parent.

passage:
Usha, that message on your phone saying you won a phone, don't click it. Sit. Your Sunaina Masi has a story.

When I was fifteen, the phone rang at home. A man said I had won a lucky draw from a big company. A television! All I had to do was pay a small "delivery fee" into a bank account, and read out the number on the back of Papa's ATM card to "verify."

I was so excited my hands were shaking. I ran to get Papa's wallet. I had the card in my hand and was about to read the numbers.

Then my Dadi, sitting in the corner, asked, "Which draw did you enter?" I hadn't entered any draw.

I put the phone down. When Papa came home, I told him everything. He said, "No real prize ever asks you to pay first. And no one real asks for those card numbers." He called the bank that evening to warn them.

Today it's OTPs, not card numbers. Same trick. Tell your mother before you do anything.

qa.q: What did the caller say young Sunaina had won?
qa.a: He said she had won a television in a lucky draw.

qa.q: What was young Sunaina feeling when she ran for Papa's wallet?
qa.a: She felt excited, her hands shaking, eager to claim the prize.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sunaina Masi's story, and why?
qa.a: Dadi's question about which draw she had entered was the turning point, because she realised she had never entered one and the offer was fake.

qa.q: How did Papa see the call when she told him?
qa.a: Papa saw it as a scam, since no real prize asks for payment first or card numbers, and he warned the bank that evening.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling a prize scam that asked for a fee and card details, recognising that real offers never ask for money or codes, and telling a parent.

passage:
Shreya's parents were at a wedding in Nashik, and she was home alone with her little brother Manoj, trying to make dinner and finish her geography project. Then her phone buzzed.

"Congratulations! You are selected for a part-time online job. Earn 3,000 daily. Pay 199 registration fee. We will send an OTP, please share it to confirm."

Three thousand a day. Shreya's heart leapt. She could buy the new geometry box, and Manoj's cycle bell. Then the OTP arrived on her mother's phone, which was linked to the family account and lying on the table.

Manoj was tugging at her sleeve, the dal was boiling over, and a second message came: "Hurry, offer expires in 5 minutes."

The hurry made her stop. Why would a real job rush her? Why would it need money and a code?

She turned off the stove and called her father. "Papa, someone is asking for the OTP on Mummy's phone for a job."

"Don't share it. Never. Block them. Well done for calling," he said. "I'll call the bank right now."

qa.q: How much registration fee did the message ask for?
qa.a: The message asked for a 199 registration fee.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she read the offer?
qa.a: Shreya felt excited and hopeful at first, then uneasy when the message rushed her.

qa.q: What did Shreya do that was wise, and why?
qa.a: Shreya stopped, did not share the OTP and called her father, because real offers never ask for money or codes and a parent could act quickly.

qa.q: How did Papa respond to Shreya's call?
qa.a: Papa told her never to share the OTP, praised her for calling and called the bank right away.

grounding: It shows a teen offered easy money for a fee and an OTP, recognising that real offers do not ask for money or codes, not sharing the OTP and telling a parent.
